This reduced the training dataset from 23,200 to 21,968 sales (5.3% removed). We retained the remaining sales, including lower-priced transactions, because a low price alone does not establish that a transaction was non-market. No test records were removed. ### Missing Value Treatment Missing predictor values were imputed using the median for numeric variables and the most frequent value for binary variables. Replacement values were calculated from the cleaned training data only. No additional training records were removed, and all training predictors now have complete values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Keep single-sale training records train_clean <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0) # The presence of numerous high-priced transactions also highlights the right-skewed nature of the housing market. These patterns suggest that sale year may be useful as a predictor, although differences in the types and locations of properties sold each year could also contribute to the observed changes. **Answer:** What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices? Our exploratory analysis highlighted four important patterns that informed our modeling approach. First, sale prices were strongly right-skewed, suggesting the need to evaluate prediction errors carefully, particularly for expensive properties. Second, building size showed a positive relationship with sale price, supporting its use as a predictor. Third, the price map revealed geographic differences, suggesting that spatial features may help explain variation in housing values. Finally, median sale prices differed across 2023–2025, indicating that sale year may also be relevant. Together, these findings motivate a model that considers property characteristics, location, and time rather than relying on a single predictor. ## Part 2 — Modeling & Feature Engineering Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`. ### Model 1 — Structural Baseline ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Model 1: Structural Baseline baseline_formula <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + garage_size + central_air + finished_basement # Fit baseline regression baseline_model <- lm( formula = baseline_formula, data = sf::st_drop_geometry(train_clean) ) # Inspect model results summary(baseline_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = baseline_formula, data = sf::st_drop_geometry(train_clean)) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -2153694 -138416 -5651 120881 9424296 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Prepare the same training observations for every model model_data <- sf::st_drop_geometry(train_clean) # Create reproducible 10-fold cross-validation splits set.seed(5080) cv_folds <- caret::createFolds( model_data$sale_price, k = 10, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE ) # Check the number of folds and their sizes length(cv_folds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sapply(cv_folds, length) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Fold01 Fold02 Fold03 Fold04 Fold05 Fold06 Fold07 Fold08 Fold09 Fold10 2196 2197 2196 2197 2195 2197 2198 2197 2197 2198 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Store predictions from all 10 validation folds cv_predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(model_data)) # Train and evaluate the baseline model on each fold for (i in seq_along(cv_folds)) { validation_rows <- cv_folds[[i]] fold_model <- lm( formula = baseline_formula, data = model_data[-validation_rows, ] ) cv_predictions[validation_rows] <- predict( fold_model, newdata = model_data[validation_rows, ] ) } # Calculate overall out-of-fold RMSE in dollars baseline_cv_rmse <- sqrt( mean((model_data$sale_price - cv_predictions)^2) ) # Display the result baseline_cv_rmse ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 292323.6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate out-of-fold prediction residuals baseline_cv_residuals <- model_data$sale_price - cv_predictions # Extract projected coordinates (EPSG:3435) train_coords <- sf::st_coordinates(train_clean) # Define 8 nearest neighbors, allowing identical coordinates baseline_knn <- spdep::knearneigh( train_coords, k = 8, use_kd_tree = FALSE ) baseline_neighbors <- spdep::knn2nb(baseline_knn) # Create row-standardized spatial weights baseline_weights <- spdep::nb2listw( baseline_neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE ) # Calculate Moran's I baseline_moran <- spdep::moran.test( baseline_cv_residuals, baseline_weights, zero.policy = TRUE ) # Display results baseline_moran ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Moran I test under randomisation data: baseline_cv_residuals weights: baseline_weights Moran I statistic standard deviate = 118.36, p-value < 0.00000000000000022 alternative hypothesis: greater sample estimates: Moran I statistic Expectation Variance 0.37755111399 -0.00004552283 0.00001017831 ``` ::: ::: ### Model 2 — Expanded Structural ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Model 2: Add four structural predictors model2_formula <- update( baseline_formula, . ~ . + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + full_basement + brick_stone_ext ) # Fit Model 2 on the cleaned training data model2 <- lm( formula = model2_formula, data = model_data ) # Generate out-of-fold predictions using the same 10 folds model2_cv_predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(model_data)) for (i in seq_along(cv_folds)) { validation_rows <- cv_folds[[i]] fold_model2 <- lm( formula = model2_formula, data = model_data[-validation_rows, ] ) model2_cv_predictions[validation_rows] <- predict( fold_model2, newdata = model_data[validation_rows, ] ) } #
